title: Mixed economy

definition.text: A mixed economy combines features of capitalism, such as private businesses, with features of socialism, such as government-run services.

facts.text: It can mean blending markets with planning, markets with state intervention, or private with public enterprise.

In the version advocated by John Maynard Keynes, private ownership and profit-seeking remain dominant, but markets are regulated and governments use fiscal and monetary policy to fight booms, busts, unemployment and inequality.
Governments in such economies provide public goods and services such as education, healthcare, infrastructure, environmental protection and management of public lands.
Most market-oriented economies today, including the United States, fall in this category, as do the Nordic countries with their extensive welfare states.
China, Norway, Singapore and Vietnam have large state-owned enterprise sectors alongside large private sectors.
Because real economies rarely match an ideal, mixed economies are usually described as leaning toward either private or public ownership.

contested_note: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek and orthodox Marxists argue there can be no lasting mixture of capitalism and socialism, since either markets or planning must drive the economy.

definition.text: Neoclassical economics is the approach that explains production, consumption and prices through supply and demand, driven by people maximizing utility and firms maximizing profit.

facts.text: It rests on three assumptions: people have rational preferences, individuals maximize utility and firms maximize profits, and people act independently with full information.
It holds that a good's value comes from its marginal utility to the user, unlike classical and Marxian economics, which use the labour theory of value.
It is the dominant approach to microeconomics; combined with Keynesian economics it formed the neoclassical synthesis that dominated mainstream economics from the 1950s.
Although it favours markets, it accepts that externalities, a form of market failure, can stop markets from producing socially desirable outcomes.
Under suitable assumptions, flexible prices allow all welfare-improving trades, so free markets yield an optimum of social welfare.
Thorstein Veblen coined the term in 1900; its shift from classical economics is often dated to Jevons and Menger (1871) and Walras (1874–1877).

title: Criticisms of neoclassical economics

definition.text: Many economists and other schools of thought criticize neoclassical economics, especially its assumptions about rational, self-interested, fully informed people.

facts.text: Marxist, behavioural, Austrian, post-Keynesian, institutionalist and other schools each differ from the neoclassical school; insiders such as Joseph Stiglitz also criticize it.
Veblen mocked its picture of a person as 'a lightning calculator of pleasures and pains'; behavioural economists study how real decisions differ from its assumptions.
Hayek argued that by assuming full information, its equilibrium models assume away the real problem of discovering knowledge spread among many people.
It is often accused of a normative bias despite claiming to be value-free, and critics call for more pluralistic teaching.
Critics say it promotes commodification and privatization because it holds that market exchange usually allocates goods best.
Defenders note it is also the main tool for assessing how policies affect inequality.

contested_note: Schools disagree over whether neoclassical assumptions and mathematical methods are sound, and whether modern mainstream models have moved beyond neoclassical economics.
